memory_candidates.content: Clause-shape audit technique: when a two-instance derivation collapses a proof (e.g. `snce_share_congr` proved from two readings of one biconditional clause at a reflexive relation), abstract it into a generic lemma over an arbitrary reflexive relation R and biconditional predicate P/Psi (`clause_shape_collapse`). Then grep-enumerate every definition in the relevant subtree containing a biconditional guarded by a universally-quantified relation, and classify each hit as intended-invariance (both sides of the <-> mention the bound variable, or no guard at all) vs. latent-collapse (Shape S: left side doesn't mention the bound variable, relation is reflexive). This mechanically finds every other instance of the same latent defect shape in a codebase, not just the one originally noticed.

GNU grep silent-failure trap: `grep -rn "pat1|pat2|pat3" ...` (no -E/-P) treats `|` as a LITERAL character in basic-regex mode, not alternation, so it returns 0 matches instead of erroring. A documented/copy-pasteable enumeration or audit command using bare `|` alternation without -E is silently broken and will report success (exit 0, empty output) rather than failing loudly. Always verify a documented grep-with-alternation command by actually re-running it, not by trusting its recorded output count.

When a research report claims an enumeration covers 'every X under subtree/**', re-verify actual subtree coverage (e.g. via `find`/`git log --diff-filter=A`) before trusting the count -- a subtree that predates the report by weeks can still be silently omitted from an ad hoc one-off scan. A re-runnable script that re-derives the count against the live tree, rather than a prose-transcribed command, catches this class of coverage gap automatically on the next run.
